title_en: Adam Posen Thinks Things Could Get Very 'Messy' for the Fed
title_zh: Peterson Institute 总裁 Adam Posen：Fed 的处境可能会变得非常'棘手'
subtitle_zh: Adam Posen 解读 Warsh 的 Jackson Hole 演讲，认为 Fed 该加息、独立性正承压。
description: Adam Posen Thinks Things Could Get Very 'Messy' for the Fed

turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots 播客。

turns.en: I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: And I'm Tracy Allaway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: Tracy, another Jackson Hole, another Jackson Hole, another Jackson Hole episode. You know, I think like with central banking and some of these topics... People are pretty polite. You know, it's like sometimes you talk to people, it's a little bit hard to know like what they're really thinking about all these topics.
turns.zh: Tracy，又是一期 Jackson Hole 特辑，又是一期 Jackson Hole，又是一期 Jackson Hole。你知道，我觉得在央行（central banking）这些话题上……大家都挺客气的。有时候你跟人聊，很难知道他们对这些话题到底是怎么想的。

turns.en: What they feel.
turns.zh: 他们真实的感受。

turns.en: It's hard to, sometimes I do perceive a certain lack of, I don't want to be.
turns.zh: 有时候我确实能感觉到某种……我不想说得那么……

turns.en: Let's say people are very diplomatic.
turns.zh: 这么说吧，大家都非常外交辞令（diplomatic）。

turns.zh: 大家都非常外交辞令。谢谢你帮我找到这个词。

turns.zh: 在 Fed 的官方场合，用这么外交辞令的方式回应你关于外交辞令的观点，本身就很外交辞令。

turns.en: People are very diplomatic, and I'm pro-diplomacy, but sometimes it's nice to just check in with someone just like, all right, let's.
turns.zh: 大家都非常外交辞令，我本人也支持外交辞令，但有时候找个人直接聊聊也挺好的，就是，好吧，咱们……

turns.en: Give it to a straight.
turns.zh: 开门见山地说。

turns.en: I'm waiting for you to describe our next guest.
turns.zh: 我等着你来介绍我们今天的嘉宾呢。

turns.en: No, I'm saying, all right, I'm just going to jump right into it.
turns.zh: 不是，我是说，好吧，我这就直接进入正题。

turns.en: No, a guest who I believe when we talk to him, I feel like here's someone who's giving it to us straight. who's not as concerned perhaps with like, you know, being overly diplomatic.
turns.zh: 是这样一位嘉宾：跟他聊的时候，我觉得这是个会跟我们开门见山的人，一个不那么在意、你知道、过于外交辞令的人。

turns.en: Someone who's not afraid to utter the words fiscal dominance.
turns.zh: 一个不怕说出'财政主导'（fiscal dominance）这几个字的人。

turns.en: Yeah, someone who's just afraid, someone who just tells it like it is.
turns.zh: 对，一个就是……一个实事求是、有一说一的人。

turns.en: Anyway, very excited to say here in Jackson Hole, back with the perfect guest, someone we've had on the podcast multiple times before, Peterson Institute President Adam Posen, also formerly a member of the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee. So Adam, thank you so much for coming back on Odd Lots.
turns.zh: 总之，很兴奋能在 Jackson Hole 这里，请回一位完美的嘉宾，一位我们之前请上过播客多次的人——Peterson Institute（彼得森国际经济研究所）总裁 Adam Posen，他还曾任 Bank of England 货币政策委员会（Monetary Policy Committee）委员。Adam，非常感谢你再次来到 Odd Lots。

turns.en: After that intro, thank you so much.
turns.zh: 听了这样的开场介绍，非常感谢你们。

turns.en: You have to really throw some fastballs.
turns.zh: 你可得给我们来点猛料（throw some fastballs）。

turns.en: I don't know whether it's hype or warning.
turns.zh: 我不知道这算是捧场还是警告。

turns.en: You have to throw some fastballs first. But what did you think of... This is the first interview we've done since the speech.
turns.zh: 你得先给我们来点猛料。不过你怎么看……这是我们在那场演讲之后做的第一个访谈。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: So what did you think of Chairman Warsh's speech?
turns.zh: 那你怎么看 Warsh 主席的这场演讲？

turns.en: I mean, even though.
turns.zh: 我是说，尽管……

turns.en: Okay, there we go.
turns.zh: 好，来了。

turns.en: No, no, no, no. Even though I knew that was the question that was coming. You know, if you were grading it, it's a B-minus speech. Okay. It's a B- speech by normal standards. It's much more positive because of the situation we were in. He, the chair, well, you know, let's be blunt, as you said. The chair had created a huge amount of not just confusion, but in central banking circles, in the sophisticated observers like you, about what he really thinks. And this was both short-term confusion Does he want to raise rates? Does he not want to raise rates? But also, medium, long term, what is behind all this task forces and the rhetoric? And then he, obviously, at the July press conference, totally messed things up. Now, to be fair, three of his four predecessors as chair had major stumbles in one of their early press conferences. Greenspan, Yellen, Powell. So in a sense, if we are able six months from now to look back And say this was a pivot point. And so the stuff that Kevin, excuse me, the chair was saying for the first few months was just growing pains. And then he got smacked by reality. Yeah. All good. Then this speech gets upgraded to a B plus and we're all happy. And I think there are a number of people now who hope that's true with some confidence more than before. Because the big thing, and Teresa and I talked briefly about this before coming on, is how different this was than last year. because last year was all about the attacks on the Fed and the fears for the independents, and the standing ovation for Jay Powell was his last thing, well, last Jackson Hole as chair. And this year, I think deliberately, the chair and the team wanted to make it much more normal, and it passed much more normal. The second thing is, as a European central banker said to me at breakfast this morning, but I think it's widely shared sentiment, for all the anti-Ford guidance, he basically set up they have to hide. Now, as you know, and we talked about a few months ago, I've been urging them to hike for a while. I think inflation's real. So again, I'm glad if they're making that call. But yeah, at this point, they really guided. Because if you read, there were four sections to the speech. In the fourth section, you basically does the litany of the reasons you would think inflation is not going to stay stable or it's going to persist and maybe go up from here, even if it goes down for a month or two for a while. And basically, the next sentence is, therefore, we have a tight new guise. Didn't say the next sentence. So things could get really messy because if they don't hike, then people start saying, was that because of Trump? Was the chair out over his skis, meaning ahead of the committee? If the chair's ahead of the committee, it's better than being behind the committee, but it's still worrisome. Then the third thing is, He did clean up some small but important things. So he had talked for a while about what's the right target. We don't really know what inflation is. And yesterday, he stated very clearly, core PCE 2%. That's the target. Similarly, he said something I think quite useful about he doesn't think wage inflation is a very good predictor of overall inflation. which is a perfectly reasonable position to take. And then later he said, I think financial conditions are important. I know you guys have talked a lot about this at the industry level. All of these were normal, sound, either mainstream or very defensible central bank things. And so that would have been sort of eh, except for the fact that we had these two months, three months of weird stuff. And so it takes on more credibility. I don't want to go on too long, but two other points, if I may. So the other two takeaways for me from the speech were, first, he does this whole second section, which is about his principles. And if I were him, I would have made this, and I was surprised, I would have made this a much narrower, much more practical speech. I basically would have cut that section.
turns.zh: 不不不不。尽管我早就知道会问这个。你知道，如果让你打分，这是一场 B- 的演讲。好。按正常标准它就是 B-。但考虑到我们当时所处的局面，它其实要正面得多。他，也就是主席，好吧，就像你说的，咱们直说吧。主席此前制造了大量的困惑，不只是在央行圈子里，也在像你这样老练的观察者当中——大家搞不清他到底怎么想。这既有短期的困惑：他到底想不想加息？也有中长期的困惑：这一堆工作组（task forces）和这些说辞背后到底是什么？然后很显然，他在七月那场记者会上把事情彻底搞砸了。话说回来，公平地讲，他前面四任主席里有三位，都在自己早期的某场记者会上出过大纰漏。Greenspan、Yellen、Powell 都是。所以从某种意义上说，如果六个月后我们能回过头来说，这是个转折点，之前几个月 Kevin——抱歉，主席——说的那些话只是成长中的阵痛，然后他被现实狠狠敲了一下，那就都好说。那这场演讲就会升级成 B+，大家都开心。我觉得现在有不少人比以往更有信心地盼着这是真的。因为关键的一点是——Teresa 和我在上节目前简短聊过——这次和去年有多不一样。去年全都是围绕对 Fed 的攻击、对独立性的担忧，还有对 Jay Powell 的起立鼓掌，那是他作为主席最后一次、呃，最后一次 Jackson Hole。而今年，我觉得是刻意地，主席和他的团队想让它恢复正常得多，实际上也确实恢复正常得多。第二点是，今早一位欧洲央行官员在早餐时跟我说——我觉得这也是普遍的看法——尽管有那么多反前瞻指引（anti-forward guidance）的表态，他其实基本上已经把话挑明：他们必须加息。你知道，几个月前我们就聊过，我一直敦促他们加息有一阵子了。我觉得通胀是实实在在的。所以如果他们真做这个决定，我也很高兴。但是，到这一步，他们其实已经给了明确指引。因为如果你读演讲，它分成四个部分。在第四部分里，他基本上罗列了一大堆理由，说明为什么你会觉得通胀不会保持稳定、会持续下去、甚至可能从这里往上走，哪怕它先回落一两个月、一段时间。而基本上，下一句就该是'因此，我们维持从紧的指引'。可那句他没说出来。所以事情可能会变得非常棘手（messy），因为如果他们不加息，人们就会开始问：那是不是因为 Trump？主席是不是抢跑（out over his skis），也就是走在了委员会前面？如果主席走在委员会前面，那比落在委员会后面要好，但仍然令人担忧。第三点是，他确实理清了一些虽小但重要的事情。此前他一直在讲，到底什么才是正确的目标，我们其实并不真正知道通胀是多少。而昨天他非常明确地表示：核心 PCE（core PCE）2%，这就是目标。类似地，他还说了一句我觉得很有用的话——他不认为工资通胀（wage inflation）是整体通胀的很好的预测指标，这是一个完全合理的立场。后来他又说，他觉得金融条件（financial conditions）很重要。我知道你们在行业层面聊过很多这个话题。这些都是正常的、稳健的、要么主流、要么非常站得住脚的央行做法。所以这些本来只能算'还行'，但正因为我们经历了这两三个月的种种怪异，它反而更具可信度了。我不想讲太久，但如果可以的话，还有另外两点。这场演讲给我的另外两个收获是：第一，他做了整整第二部分，讲的是他的原则。如果我是他——这一点让我挺意外——我会把这场演讲做得窄得多、务实得多。我基本上会把第二部分整段砍掉。

turns.en: It was a long speech for someone who says they don't like forward guidance.
turns.zh: 对一个说自己不喜欢前瞻指引（forward guidance）的人来说，这演讲挺长的。

turns.en: Exactly. No, you're absolutely right, Tracy. I was like, people asked me ahead of time what I thought was going to happen. I thought he was going to compete with Jay Powell from like four years ago for the shortest possible speech. I thought he was just going to, you know, he didn't. So I think that muddles his message because some of the principal stuff, it raises more questions than answers. It's either a bromide or what does he really mean by that? And I don't think that was useful. But, you know, that's not a big deal. The big deal that I'm worried about is, and a lot of ex-Fed, ex-Central Bank people, academics are worried about, is he seems to be still, even through yesterday's speech for all its improvements, trying to maximize his last-minute discretion. Yeah.
turns.zh: 没错。不，你说得完全对，Tracy。我当时就想，有人提前问我我觉得会发生什么。我以为他会去跟大约四年前的 Jay Powell 比拼谁的演讲最短。我以为他就会……你知道，结果他没有。所以我觉得这反而让他的信息变得含糊，因为其中一些关于原则的东西，它引出的问题比答案还多。要么是一句陈词滥调（bromide），要么就是他这话到底什么意思？我觉得那没什么用。不过，这不是大事。真正让我担心的大事——也是很多 Fed 前官员、央行前官员、学者担心的——是即便经过昨天这场虽有诸多改进的演讲，他似乎仍然在试图把自己临场斟酌（last-minute discretion）的空间最大化。是的。

turns.en: So this is the thing I noticed, because at the very end of the speech, he talks about, well, inflation has to be heading in the right direction and at the right speed. And... I don't know what the right speed is. The right speed sounds very subjective to me.
turns.zh: 这就是我注意到的一点，因为在演讲的最后，他说，嗯，通胀必须朝着正确的方向、以正确的速度回落。而……我不知道什么叫正确的速度。'正确的速度'听起来非常主观。

turns.en: Absolutely. And right direction doesn't mean anything unless you're saying the target. I mean, without the speed, just to emphasize your point, without the speed, then we're back with what we had the last four years, which is inflation's above target. Well, we know what the direction should be, but if we don't declare a speed, we're going to bring it back to target. It doesn't mean anything. Right. So yeah, I think it's really striking because that, to me, is the most consistent thing through the stuff he said from his hearings, his confirmation hearings, his first two press conferences, his remarks at ECB Cintra and then yesterday. He's sort of reserving the right to make up his mind at the last minute, before every meeting, without pre-committing. what things he's looking at. He gave us a little bit of that, I mean, to his credit. He did say some things about which indicators he likes better than others, and that's good. And you don't want him to be inflexible. But it's really odd for somebody coming from the Hoover Institution, who's been seen as a conservative, who was mentored by the late John Taylor, but also just in a broader central banking context, everybody tries to situate themselves between what's called rules versus discretion. Is it like, I'm going to raise rates every time monetary growth goes up or something like that, which generally is a bad idea if you're too strict. Or pure discretion. I'm going to, you know, I don't have to justify. I'm just going to make the right call every time. And that's basically Greenspan circa 1999. And Greenspan could get away with it, partly because he was very good and partly because by that point he had such dominance over the committee. And partly it caused trouble for later. because then you had the weekend at Bernie's problem, which is if Greenspan, God forbid, drops dead, and we obviously just lost him recently, but in 1999... I have.
turns.zh: 完全同意。而且'正确的方向'其实没什么意义，除非你说明目标是多少。我是说，没有速度——再强调一下你的观点——没有速度，我们就又回到了过去四年的状态：通胀高于目标。好吧，我们知道方向应该是什么，但如果不宣布一个速度、说我们要把通胀拉回目标，那这句话就毫无意义。对吧。所以，是的，我觉得特别引人注目（striking）的是，对我来说，这是从他的一系列表态里最一以贯之的东西——从他的提名听证会（confirmation hearings）、他头两场记者会、他在 ECB Sintra 论坛的讲话，一直到昨天。他有点像在保留一种权利：在每次会议之前的最后一刻才拿定主意，而不预先承诺他到底在看哪些东西。他倒是给了我们一点点这方面的信息——这一点得肯定他。他确实说了一些他更看重哪些指标、不那么看重哪些，这是好事。你也不希望他太死板。但对于一个来自 Hoover Institution、被视为保守派、由已故的 John Taylor 一手带出来的人来说，这真的很奇怪。而且放到更宽泛的央行语境里也一样：每个人都要给自己在所谓'规则 versus 斟酌'（rules versus discretion）之间找个定位。是说'我每次货币增长上去就加息'之类的——如果你太严格，那通常是个坏主意；还是纯粹的斟酌——'我不用给出理由，我每次都能做对判断'。后者基本上就是 1999 年前后的 Greenspan。Greenspan 能这么干，一部分是因为他确实很厉害，一部分是因为到那时他对委员会已经有了极强的掌控力。而这也在一定程度上给后来埋下了麻烦。因为那样你就有了'周末去 Bernie 家'（weekend at Bernie's）式的难题：万一 Greenspan——老天保佑别这样——突然离世……我们显然最近才刚失去他，但在 1999 年……我有……

turns.en: The image in my head now.
turns.zh: 我现在脑子里就有那个画面了。

turns.en: No, no. In 1999, you were worried if then already somewhat old Alan Greenspan had a heart attack on the Fed's tennis court, all the credibility went away because it was all about him. Oh, interesting. And this is why Ben Bernanke, Rick Mishkin, Thomas Laubach, and I pushed the inflation targeting idea. And Ben very consciously, when he was chair, pushed accountability because he wanted it to be not just all about one person. And I think this, to me, is not talked about enough and is the most worrying thing about where Chair Warsh has gone.
turns.zh: 不，不。在 1999 年，你会担心，如果当时已经不算年轻的 Alan Greenspan 在 Fed 的网球场上心脏病发作，那所有的公信力就都没了，因为一切都系于他一人。哦，有意思。这正是为什么 Ben Bernanke、Rick Mishkin、Thomas Laubach 和我一起推动通胀目标制（inflation targeting）这个理念。Ben 在担任主席时非常有意识地推动问责制（accountability），因为他希望这套体系不要只系于某一个人。而在我看来，这一点被讨论得太少，也是 Warsh 主席目前走向里最令人担忧的地方。

turns.en: So this is exactly what my next question was going to be. You have been a central banker. at the boe not necessarily the fed but you have insight into how these monetary policy making committees actually work what is the role of the fed chair in its current form as you envision it is warsh supposed to be trying to get everyone on his side and get them voting in his direction or is he supposed to be a I don't know, synthesizing a common position from the committee?
turns.zh: 这正是我接下来要问的。你当过央行官员，是在 Bank of England（boe），不一定是 Fed，但你对这些货币政策决策委员会实际如何运作有洞见。在你看来，如今形态下的 Fed 主席这个角色到底是什么？Warsh 是不是应该努力争取每个人都站到他这边、按他的方向投票，还是说他应该——我不知道——从委员会里综合出一个共同立场？

turns.en: That's a really good question, Tracy. And in the Fed system, that's not specified. And it varies over time, partly because of the chair, partly because of the political surroundings, partly because of the economy. But for example, at the European Central Bank, it is, for all the attention deservedly President Lagarde gets, It is very much meant to be a consensus-driven organization and really try to get as many people on board as possible. And that's partly because they're representing nations, not districts within one nation. At the Bank of England, when I served, and still, and this is something Chair Warsh invokes now, invokes, I should say, is it's all about discussion, what Kevin calls friendly debate or whatever.
turns.zh: 这是个非常好的问题，Tracy。在 Fed 体系里，这一点并没有明确规定。而且它随时间变化，一部分取决于主席本人，一部分取决于政治环境，一部分取决于经济。但比如说，在 European Central Bank，尽管 President Lagarde 理应受到那么多关注，它在设计上非常强调共识驱动（consensus-driven），真的要尽可能争取更多人达成一致。这部分是因为他们代表的是各个国家，而不是一个国家内部的不同地区。在 Bank of England，我任职的时候是这样，现在也还是——这一点正是 Warsh 主席现在搬出来讲的，我是说，他强调的是一切都靠讨论，也就是 Kevin 所谓的'友好辩论'之类的。

turns.en: The family fight.
turns.zh: '家庭内部的争执'（family fight）。

turns.en: Yeah, that's what he says. You're right. And the Bank of England really prioritizes that. The Fed has generally, on average, given more power and deference to the chair, certainly basically since Volcker, so the last 45 years. It varies over time, but essentially there's always something. So a financial crisis, Ben Bernanke wanted, started running the committee trying to open it up more, more debate, but financial crisis came and you really wanted been making the decisions and there wasn't time. And then there were these crazy US rules about you can't have more than four people in the room from the committee at one time without it becoming a public.
turns.zh: 对，他就是这么说的。你说得没错。Bank of England 确实非常看重这一点。而 Fed 一般来说、平均而言，给了主席更多权力和尊重，基本上从 Volcker 起就是这样，也就是过去 45 年。它随时间变化，但本质上总会有一些状况。比如金融危机时，Ben Bernanke 本想、开始试着把委员会运作得更开放、更多辩论，但金融危机来了，你真的需要 Ben 来做决定，根本没时间。然后美国还有这些荒唐的规定：委员会里同一时间在一个房间不能超过四个人，否则就变成一场公开……

turns.en: Then you have to take notes, right?
turns.zh: 然后你就得做会议记录，对吧？

turns.en: Then you have to take notes and whatever. And so like ended up, it would be the New York Fed president, Chair Bernanke, Kevin Warsh, and Don Cohn were the four people in the room. And that was the right call given the situation. So anyway, this is part of the reason I worry about the discretion because The ethic of the committee and the norm of the committee in the Fed system is you don't contradict the chair. You might dissent. But even there, as was pointed out by the former Fed governor, Larry Meyer, a while back, there's sort of an informal rule. Only so many people dissent on the committee at any one meeting. And the chair never loses a vote. Even Volcker, once it was clear he was going to lose a vote, He basically said, next meeting is my last meeting.
turns.zh: 然后你就得做记录什么的。所以最后，房间里的四个人会是 New York Fed 主席、Bernanke 主席、Kevin Warsh 和 Don Cohn。鉴于当时的情况，这是正确的安排。总之，这也是我担心斟酌权（discretion）的部分原因，因为在 Fed 体系里，委员会的伦理和规范是：你不要跟主席唱反调。你可以投反对票（dissent）。但即便如此，正如 Fed 前理事 Larry Meyer 早些时候指出的，这里有种不成文的规矩：任何一次会议上，委员会里投反对票的人数是有上限的。而且主席从来不会输掉一次投票。哪怕是 Volcker，一旦眼看要输掉一次投票，他基本上就会说，下次会议就是我最后一次会议了。

turns.en: That's super interesting.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。

turns.en: Well, let's actually– so one of the comments Chairman Walsh said, he basically said, I don't know, 64, 65 months of above target inflation.
turns.zh: 那么，其实——Warsh 主席说过一句话，他大概说的是，64、65 个月的通胀高于目标。

turns.en: That's true.
turns.zh: 这是事实。

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But he also said, and this is the Fed's fault.
turns.zh: 但他还说，这是 Fed 的错。

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And so, you know, obviously– That means it's in large part he claims his predecessor's fault. But it also occurs to me, you know, inflation has been above target around the world in many respects, and it's not just a U.S.
turns.zh: 所以，你知道，显然——这意味着他在很大程度上把责任归给了他的前任。但我也想到，你知道，在很多方面，全球各地的通胀都一直高于目标，这不只是美国一个……

turns.en: Problem. I'm curious, like that comment, like, is it seems kind of true? Like, is that is that fair?
turns.zh: ……的问题。我很好奇，那番话，听起来好像有点道理？这么说、这么说公允吗？

turns.en: Is that correct? I think it's fair. I mean, I think what was unfair in the run up to his appointment by President Trump and in some of the initial statements, there was. A lot of talk about diplomatic, not diplomatic. There was a lot of pretty nasty sounding tone about the previous regime. And, you know, I'm going to reform, I'm going to clean house on my watch. It's okay. That was unnecessary, but I do think it is entirely justified to say, um, care pal with the deference and buy-in of the committee. Basically start was late to the game and hiking and 2022. was early, if not, in my view, profoundly mistaken to cut multiple times last year and is behind the curve again. And the international comparison actually doesn't flatter the US. You have to do a little bit of careful things on the data. But basically, if you control for three things, which is how dependent on imported energy are you, how What was the inflation going into the last few years? So what do you have to clean up from the predecessor? And then out of the Fed or any centralized control, how loose is your fiscal policy? When you look at that, the Fed is more of an outlier. So the ECBs kept inflation down. The Swiss National Bank's kept inflation relatively down. Bank of England's almost the same as the Fed. But additionally, This gets into the independent stuff because part of the reason the US has more inflation in my view and many people's view is because Biden did do a fiscal blowout on coming into office that probably wasn't necessary. And then there's been no consolidation. And obviously Trump in his first year did this long-term set of tax cuts. And so, but again, it's still, if you take Kevin's, what you quoted him, you know, it's ultimately up to the Fed. If you take that seriously, then all this fiscal laxity in discipline should be another reason to hike. Yeah, yeah. So anyway, much too long, but I think even a sober, temperate thing suggests, no, Powell did get it wrong. Now, it's not he got it horrendously wrong. It's not he got it wrong for the wrong reasons. But, you know, when you and I talked The three of us talked about this last year, which is, and the year before, that at Jackson Hole there was this drumbeat from the Fed staff and members. The labor markets could be really weak. The inflation is going down. And there were people like me or Michael Strain, AEI, and Diane Swank in KPMG who were out there saying, we don't see this. Now, I'm not saying necessarily they had to listen to us and it didn't. but just to say they actually did get something wrong. There were people who were saying, no, the labor market is not going to collapse in the next two years. And they kept saying, yes, it will. So yeah, they did get some things wrong.
turns.zh: 这么说对不对？我觉得公允。我是说，我觉得在 Trump 总统提名他之前、以及最初的一些表态里，有些东西是不公允的。有大量关于外交辞令不外交辞令的讨论。对上一任班子，有很多听起来相当刻薄的口吻。你知道，'我要改革，我要在我任内清理门户'。这样也可以。那其实没必要。但我确实认为，这么说完全是站得住脚的：呃，恕我直言，在委员会的尊重和认同之下，基本上——2022 年加息入场太晚；去年多次降息，即便不算、在我看来是严重错误，那也是过早；而且现在又落后于形势（behind the curve）了。而国际比较其实并不给美国长脸。你在数据上得做一些细致的处理。但基本上，如果你控制住三个因素：一是你对进口能源的依赖程度；二是过去几年之前你的通胀是多少，也就是你得替前任收拾多少烂摊子；三是在 Fed 或任何集中控制之外，你的财政政策有多宽松（loose）。把这些考虑进去后，Fed 反而更像是一个异类（outlier）。ECB 把通胀压住了。Swiss National Bank 也把通胀相对压住了。Bank of England 几乎和 Fed 一样。但此外——这就牵涉到独立性的问题了——因为在我和很多人看来，美国通胀更高的部分原因在于，Biden 上任时确实搞了一轮财政大放水（fiscal blowout），那很可能没必要。然后一直没有财政整顿（consolidation）。而显然 Trump 在第一年就推出了这一整套长期减税。所以，还是那句话，如果你认真对待 Kevin——也就是你引用的他那句话——你知道，最终还是取决于 Fed。如果你把这当回事，那么所有这些财政上的松懈和缺乏纪律，就应该是又一个加息的理由。是，是。总之，讲得太长了，但我觉得即便用一个冷静、温和的判断来看，结论也是：不，Powell 确实搞错了。倒不是说他错得离谱，也不是说他错的原因不对。但是，你知道，去年和前年，当我们三个聊起这个的时候——在 Jackson Hole，Fed 的官员和委员们一直在反复敲这个鼓点：劳动力市场可能会非常疲弱，通胀正在下行。而像我、AEI 的 Michael Strain、KPMG 的 Diane Swank 这些人则在外面说，我们看不到这种情况。我不是说他们非得听我们的、结果也没听，只是说他们确实把一些事情判断错了。当时有人在说，不，劳动力市场在未来两年不会崩塌。而他们却一直说，会的，它会崩。所以，是的，他们确实把一些事情搞错了。

turns.en: What's the sort of bar for political interference with the Fed? Because it could be anything from just the president talking about how he thinks rates are artificially high. It could be maybe something a little bit different, like The fiscal dominance idea to the extent that the Fed now feels hamstrung in some way in terms of what it can do with rates.
turns.zh: 政治干预 Fed 的门槛到底在哪儿？因为它可以是任何程度的东西：小到总统只是谈论他觉得利率被人为压得过高；也可能是稍微不同的一点，比如'财政主导'（fiscal dominance）这个概念——如果 Fed 现在在某种程度上觉得自己在利率上被束手束脚的话。

turns.en: Again, you're right to raise that, Tracy. I mean, so the first thing to say is a certain amount of yelling at or scapegoating the Fed is part of the game. And in fact, in previous presidencies, it kind of sometimes was healthy, right? So it's like, oh, God, Fed has to raise rates to deal with inflation. I don't want to be blamed for it. So I'm going to go out there and yell. But meanwhile, in the background, wink, wink, Fed, do your job. And that was under Volcker, under Greenspan, under Bernanke, under Yellen. I mean, that was always understood. So a certain amount of, not like President Trump tweeting the Fed chair is an enemy of the state, not using lawfare to go after Lisa, Governor Cook, or now Governor Powell. I mean, that's outrageous and arguably criminal. But certain amount of carping about the central bank, that's fine. Where the rubber hits the road is partly what you said, which is when does the government treasury secretary or president who's trying to sell U.S. bonds say, you have to help me sell U.S. bonds, whether or not inflation's high. And in that case, what a central banker should do, a Fed president or a Fed governor should do is say, I'm here to help you sell U.S. bonds and your successor sell U.S. bonds and your successor sell U.S. bonds. And that means I don't do cheating and manipulation now. I'm here to help you sell the bonds.
turns.zh: 同样，你提这点很对，Tracy。我是说，首先要讲的是，对 Fed 一定程度的叫骂或甩锅（scapegoating），本身就是游戏的一部分。而且事实上，在过去几任总统任内，这有时还挺健康的，对吧？就是说，'天啊，Fed 得加息来对付通胀，我可不想为此背锅，所以我要出去嚷嚷'。但与此同时，在暗地里，眨眨眼，'Fed，你干你的活儿'。Volcker 时期、Greenspan 时期、Bernanke 时期、Yellen 时期都是这样。我是说，这一直是心照不宣的。所以一定程度的——不是像 Trump 总统发推说 Fed 主席是国家公敌，不是用'法律战'（lawfare）去对付 Lisa、Cook 理事，或者现在的 Powell 理事。我是说，那种做法令人发指，甚至可以说构成犯罪。但对央行一定程度的挑剔抱怨，那没关系。真正见真章的地方（where the rubber hits the road），部分就是你说的那个：什么时候，那位想卖出美国国债的政府财政部长或总统会说，'不管通胀高不高，你都得帮我卖美国国债'。在那种情况下，一位央行官员——一位 Fed 主席或 Fed 理事——应该说：'我在这里是要帮你卖美国国债，帮你的继任者卖美国国债，再帮你的继任者卖美国国债。这意味着我现在不搞作弊和操纵。我是在帮你把国债卖出去。'

turns.en: You're preserving the long-term credibility of U.S.
turns.zh: 你是在维护美国……的长期公信力。

turns.en: Debt. And so you have to be willing to stand up to that. And that gets us into the potential really big situation now. But the second thing, and this is the part that was really unprecedented under Trump besides the individual illegal attacks on individual members, is they were, and this was very loud last year, they were threatening to take away the votes of some of the Reserve Bank presidents or quickly turn over the Reserve Bank presidents, not get rid of them and put in their own political appointees rather than having the staggered terms as intended. And there was talk about changing the Fed's mandate and there was And then the things about the Fed's budget. And so the big one, economically speaking, is the caving in in the face of fiscal pressure. But the almost as big and as a means to that one is the threats to politicize, turn over, fire, remove the functional independence of the Fed by messing with who's appointed when.
turns.zh: ……国债（的长期公信力）。所以你得愿意顶住那种压力。这就把我们带到了眼下这个可能非常严重的局面。但第二点——除了针对个别委员的那些非法攻击之外，这才是 Trump 任内真正前所未有部分——是他们（去年这一点闹得很响）在威胁要剥夺一些 Reserve Bank（储备银行）主席的投票权，或者迅速把 Reserve Bank 主席们换掉、赶走他们、安插自己的政治任命人选，而不是像原本设计的那样让他们错开任期（staggered terms）。当时还有关于修改 Fed 使命（mandate）的讨论，以及关于 Fed 预算的那些事。所以从经济上说，最大的问题是在财政压力面前屈服。而几乎同样严重、并且是通向那个问题的手段，是那些威胁：通过操纵'什么时候任命什么人'，把 Fed 政治化、大换血、解雇、剥夺 Fed 的实际独立性（functional independence）。

turns.en: It occurs to me, you're talking about this phrase, family fight. And I hadn't thought much about it, because it's a good sounding phrase. It's like, great, we want our- You want healthy debate.
turns.zh: 我突然想到，你提到'家庭内部的争执'（family fight）这个说法。我之前没太在意，因为它听着挺不错的。就是，太好了，我们想要……你想要健康的辩论。

turns.en: It feels good, right? You want healthy debate.
turns.zh: 听着挺舒服的，对吧？你想要健康的辩论。

turns.en: It feels good, but he's used the phrase a bunch of times now in both of his press conferences, I believe. And I'm curious now, just sort of thinking about a few things that have been said, Last year at this conference, I asked Chicago Fed President Austin Goolsbee, why are dissents rare at the Fed? And one of his answers is that Chairman Powell was good at building consensus.
turns.zh: 听着舒服，但我记得他在两场记者会上都用过好几次这个说法了。现在我就很好奇，结合说过的一些话——去年在这个会议上，我问 Chicago Fed 主席 Austin Goolsbee，为什么 Fed 里投反对票这么罕见？他的一个回答是，Powell 主席很擅长建立共识。

turns.en: But now I'm sort.
turns.zh: 但现在我有点……

turns.en: Of curious, was there a perception under the Powell years that he was too good at building consensus? Did members of the FOMC feel that actually that meeting room was not a real site for debate? And when Kevin Warsh says we want the family fight. Is he saying, no, I'm okay with, unlike my predecessor, I'm actually okay if you don't agree with me?
turns.zh: ……好奇，在 Powell 那几年，是否有种看法觉得他太擅长建立共识了？FOMC 的委员们是否觉得，那间会议室其实并不是一个真正用来辩论的场所？而当 Kevin Warsh 说'我们想要家庭内部的争执'时，他是不是在说，不，跟我的前任不一样，如果你们不同意我，我其实是接受的？

turns.en: I think he's saying, I think Kevin Warsh is saying what you just said, Joe, that I am okay with more dissent and more debate. I don't believe him. Okay. But if you take it at face value, he's right. and that's what I meant in part.
turns.zh: 我觉得他说的、我觉得 Kevin Warsh 说的就是你刚说的那个意思，Joe：我接受更多反对票和更多辩论。我不信他。好吧。但如果你照字面接受，他是对的，这也部分是我刚才的意思。

turns.en: You think he's right?
turns.zh: 你觉得他说得对？

turns.en: He's right that debate had gotten too little, and it's healthy to have debate. I think, Paul, it's partly he was very good inside the building, but I think it was two other things. I think he smartly and justifiably, first under COVID, and then when the Fed was under such overt attack by Trump, saying, let's not dissent and create divisions in the committee casually. Let's make the bar very high. If you dissent, I understand, but let's not show division because that just gives the attackers on the Fed, or in the case of COVID, that just gives the sense of panic. And there is always this temptation. So when I was on the Bank of England MPC, which was 2009 to 12, so I was there during the financial crisis. And there was a point at which the governor and Bank of England had a much more lively debate. publicly at least, than the Fed. Then Governor Mervyn King came at one point and said, look, quantitative easing is really controversial. We're going to take the vote. You'll vote however you want. But once we've done it, can we have a moratorium on people asking whether or not quantitative easing works or not for a while? And I totally supported that. I mean, again, it's an emergency. You don't want to just Oh, well, you know, according to VIXELL, I'm not sure, you know, the usual central bank thing. I'm giving a talk in Glasgow and I just sort of wander off into monetary theory. So I think not through bad motivations, but I think Powell ended up between the COVID panic and then the rallying solidarity and people not wanting to look like they were undermining the chairman while the Fed was under attack. You did end up getting much lower than usual dissents. And then what happens is which shouldn't but does happen, is it builds momentum. So if you've gone 12 meetings, 15 meetings without anybody dissenting, the bar psychologically becomes higher for someone to dissent. So again, I hope I'm wrong. I don't think Chair Warsh really means it. I hope he does. But taking it literally, yeah, we went through a period where there was too little dissent.
turns.zh: 他说得对的一点是，辩论曾经太少，而有辩论是健康的。我觉得，就 Powell 而言，这部分是因为他在机构内部做得很好，但我觉得还有另外两个原因。我觉得他很明智、也很正当地，先是在 COVID 期间，然后是在 Fed 受到 Trump 如此公开攻击的时候，说：'咱们别轻易投反对票、别在委员会里制造分裂。咱们把门槛定得很高。你要投反对票，我理解，但咱们别表现出分裂，因为那只会给攻击 Fed 的人递刀子；或者在 COVID 的情况下，只会营造出一种恐慌感。'而这种诱惑一直存在。所以我在 Bank of England 货币政策委员会（MPC）任职时——那是 2009 到 2012 年，也就是金融危机期间我在任——有一段时间，行长和 Bank of England 公开地看，其辩论要比 Fed 活跃得多。然后 Mervyn King 行长有一次出来说：'听着，量化宽松（quantitative easing）真的很有争议。我们要投票了，你们想怎么投就怎么投。但一旦投完，我们能不能在一段时间内，暂停大家去争论量化宽松到底管不管用？'我完全支持这个做法。我是说，那毕竟是紧急状态。你不希望出现那种'哦，这个嘛，你知道，按照 VIXELL 的说法，我也说不准'——就是央行那套老掉牙的腔调。我在 Glasgow 做一场演讲，结果就飘到货币理论上去了。所以我觉得，并非出于坏动机，而是 Powell 最终夹在 COVID 的恐慌、以及后来那种同仇敌忾的团结之间——在 Fed 受攻击时，大家都不想显得像是在拆主席的台。结果就是，反对票确实比平时少了很多。然后接下来发生的、本不该发生却确实发生的事，是它会累积成惯性。所以如果你已经开了 12 次、15 次会议都没人投反对票，那从心理上，某人要投反对票的门槛就变高了。所以再说一次，我希望我是错的。我不觉得 Warsh 主席是真心这么想的。我希望他是。但照字面理解，是的，我们确实经历了一段反对票太少的时期。

turns.en: So you mentioned Mervyn King just then, and King is heading the new task force on Fed communications. So I'm curious whether you have any insights or perhaps informed guesses about what the problem is that Warsh slash King are now trying to solve.
turns.zh: 你刚提到 Mervyn King，而 King 正在牵头 Fed 沟通（communications）方面的新工作组。所以我很好奇，对于 Warsh／King 现在想解决的问题到底是什么，你有没有什么洞见，或者至少有根据的猜测？

turns.en: Well, I know well two of the three members of that committee. So I worked with Governor King. He was governor before that when I was at the Bank of England. And Peter Fisher, the former New York Fed and U.S. Treasury senior official, is on the board of directors of the Peterson Institute. So just full disclosure. So I've not talked to them directly about confidential things, but just disclosure. I think this is the committee that has the biggest chance of a surprise to being radical. I think people are very concentrated on the balance sheet committee, and I think actually they are likely to come out with much more sober, practical, smaller scale recommendations than people think they are. That's just my guess. But knowing who's on that committee, Raghu Rajan, Jennifer Einstein, Karen Dinan, who's also a colleague of mine. But I think the communications fund is going to surprise people. Because both Mervyn and Peter, and I'm only referring to their public statements, have gotten pretty radically skeptical about central bank communications in recent years. So Mervyn King was actually the leader of the inflation targeting movement long before we wrote our book. He's the one who in 1992, when the British pound fell out of the exchange rate mechanism and there was basically a crisis, we need to have something to anchor in the UK. He's the one who leapt into action with a couple of key staffers. He was chief economist of the bank at the time. and said, look, these little countries are trying inflation targeting, but we think it can work for us, and he did. And so he was the father, the parent, of what used to be known as the fan charts. I love the fan charts.
turns.zh: 嗯，那个委员会三名成员里有两名我很熟。我跟 King 行长共事过。我在 Bank of England 时他先是行长。还有 Peter Fisher——曾任 New York Fed 和美国财政部（U.S. Treasury）高级官员——是 Peterson Institute 的董事会成员。所以我先做个充分披露（full disclosure）。我没有就机密的事情直接跟他们谈过，只是披露一下。我觉得这个委员会最有可能带来意外、走向激进。我认为大家的注意力都集中在资产负债表委员会（balance sheet committee）上，而我觉得他们实际上更可能拿出比大家预想的冷静得多、务实得多、规模小得多的建议。这只是我的猜测。但看看那个委员会都有谁——Raghu Rajan、Jennifer Einstein、Karen Dinan，她也是我的同事。但我觉得沟通委员会会让人意外。因为 Mervyn 和 Peter 两人——我这里只引用他们的公开表态——近年来对央行沟通都变得相当激进地怀疑。Mervyn King 其实在我们写那本书之前很久，就是通胀目标制运动的领军人物。1992 年，当英镑脱离汇率机制（exchange rate mechanism）、基本上陷入危机、英国需要一个东西来锚定时，就是他带着几位关键幕僚迅速行动起来——他当时是该行的首席经济学家——说：'听着，这些小国在尝试通胀目标制，但我们觉得它对我们也能行得通。'他就这么做了。所以他是过去所谓'扇形图'（fan charts）之父、之母。我很喜欢扇形图。

turns.en: I think I was the only one, but I really liked it.
turns.zh: 我觉得我是唯一喜欢它的人，但我真的很喜欢。

turns.en: No, no, no, there were a few of us scattered around, but it was definitely a niche product. And there are problems, better or worse, with fan charts, and the Bank of England has changed it. But basically, Mervyn... was leading the effort, and we cited this hugely, Bernanke et al. cited this hugely in our book, that they were, again, back to the combination of accountability and transparency, that you were sending out a forecast. You were being much more explicit than central banks usually were about the forecast. You were with the fan charts, which are essentially colored spreads about how likely a given outcome would be. Here's what we centrally think is going to happen. Here's what may happen. You were trying to give the message this was probabilistic, that we're making our best guess, but it's probably going to err on the high side, and it's going to be somewhere around here. So anyway, it was very, very much about transparency, accountability, and more information is better. Regular information is better. Commitment to specific releases at specific times is better. So you have a track record, and the committee has to admit when it changes its mind or learns something. Anyway, in more recent years, since Governor King left the bank, retired, he's become quite loud in the spirit of some of the things Chair Warsh has been saying, that it's too much noise, central banks can't forecast, we're lousy at forecasting, given that we shouldn't be putting out all this information that's not really misleading, and Mervyn also, from even before that, was very concerned about this idea of the markets getting too dependent on the information and the future plans of the central bank and then not giving as much information back and also having more moral hazard that they're not going to take the price and risk.
turns.zh: 不，不，不，我们这拨人零散地还是有几个的，但它绝对是个小众产品。扇形图有它的问题，有好有坏，Bank of England 后来也改了。但基本上，Mervyn……在牵头推动这件事，我们大量引用了它，Bernanke 等人在我们的书里也大量引用，说的还是问责（accountability）与透明（transparency）的结合：你要发布一份预测；你在预测方面要比央行通常的做法明确得多；你用扇形图——它本质上是用不同颜色的区间来表示某个结果出现的可能性有多大。'这是我们中心判断认为会发生的情况，这是可能会发生的情况。'你想传达的信息是：这是概率性的，我们是在做最优猜测，但它很可能偏向上侧，大致会落在这个范围附近。所以，总之，这非常非常强调透明、问责，以及'更多信息更好'。定期发布信息更好；承诺在特定时间做特定发布更好。这样你就有了一份过往记录（track record），委员会在改变想法或学到新东西时就必须承认。总之，近些年，自从 King 行长离任、退休以来，他变得相当高调，其精神与 Warsh 主席一直讲的一些说法一致：噪声太多了，央行没法预测，我们预测得很烂，既然如此我们就不该发布这么多其实具有误导性的信息。而且 Mervyn 甚至更早就非常担心这样一个问题：市场对央行的信息和未来计划变得过度依赖，然后自己却不回馈同样多的信息，同时还产生更多道德风险（moral hazard）——他们不会去承担定价和风险。

turns.en: This is the idea that yields are an important policy signal for central bankers, or they should be.
turns.zh: 这就是那个观点：收益率（yields）对央行官员来说是一个重要的政策信号，或者说它本应是。

turns.en: They should be. And it should be a two-way street. It should be yields and volatility around yields should be higher than it had been. This is their point of view, not mine. It should be higher than it had been because that forces markets to take risk more seriously and price things better. And so you have less, not zero, but you have less chance of a bubble and less inequality of things running out of them. And then at the same time, that should mean the pricing that the markets give you is more informative. And Peter Fisher, who, after he was at Fed New York and Treasury, was head of Asia and other senior roles at BlackRock, he feels very strongly these two points as well, at least what I know from his public statements. He's very skeptical about central banks' ability to forecast and very worried about central banks' certainty about central banks causing bubbles and indiscipline and then clouding market signals. So even though Chair Warsh in the speech here at Jackson Hole backed off a little bit of some of the more extreme statements of that, he admitted that he had this thing about a hall of mirrors image in the speech, which is a way of admitting that the market isn't always right. And if the Fed chases the market noise, you may get a weird dynamic. And I was glad he said that. Much better than play the ball, not the referee, which was garbage.
turns.zh: 它本应是。而且这应该是一条双向的道路（two-way street）。应该是收益率、以及围绕收益率的波动率，都比过去更高一些。这是他们的观点，不是我的。它应该比过去更高，因为那会迫使市场更认真地对待风险、更好地定价。这样一来，你出现泡沫的概率就更小——不是零，但更小——各种失控的情况也更少。与此同时，这也应该意味着市场给你的定价更具信息量。而 Peter Fisher——他在 Fed New York 和财政部之后，曾在 BlackRock 担任亚洲区主管及其他高级职务——他对这两点也感触很深，至少从他的公开表态我是这么了解的。他对央行的预测能力非常怀疑，也非常担心央行那种笃定、担心央行会制造泡沫和缺乏纪律，进而扰乱市场信号。所以，尽管 Warsh 主席在这里 Jackson Hole 的演讲中，对其中一些更极端的说法稍微往回收了一点——他承认自己在演讲里用了'镜厅'（hall of mirrors）这个意象，这其实是承认市场并不总是对的，而如果 Fed 去追逐市场的噪声，你可能会陷入一种诡异的动态——我很高兴他说了这个。这比那句'盯球，别盯裁判'（play the ball, not the referee）好多了，那句话就是垃圾。

turns.en: That was the previous message was like, oh, market, you're the ball, like off you go.
turns.zh: 之前那套信息给人的感觉就是，哦，市场，你就是那个球，去吧。

turns.en: Yeah, that was really bad. But anyway, no, I mean, of all the things that annoyed the central banking community, that may have been the most annoying. But anyway, so just to say, I think Chair Warsh's true beliefs and instincts, though, are much more in the we can't get any forecasts right. Market has much more information on a lot of things than we do. We have a moral hazard issue of not spoon-feeding the markets. So I think the communications committee is probably where we're going to get the biggest surprises.
turns.zh: 对，那真的很糟糕。不过总之，我是说，在所有让央行圈子恼火的事情里，那件可能是最恼人的。总之，我只是想说，我觉得 Warsh 主席真正的信念和直觉，其实更接近于'我们没法把任何预测做对；市场在很多事情上掌握的信息比我们多得多；我们存在一个不该把饭喂到市场嘴边（spoon-feeding）的道德风险问题'。所以我觉得，沟通委员会很可能才是我们会看到最大意外的地方。

turns.en: Yeah, I find myself like thinking like maybe all these things, various charts, dots, et cetera, like served a real purpose maybe post-GFC and maybe it's just a lot of noise right now. Since we're talking about this sort of monetary policy at the theoretical level and a lot of– which is great.
turns.zh: 是啊，我发现自己在想，也许所有这些东西——各种图表、点阵图（dots）等等——在全球金融危机（GFC）之后那段时间确实起到了真正的作用，但现在可能只是一堆噪声。既然我们在理论层面聊货币政策，还有很多——这很好。

turns.en: Oh, yeah. And all this.
turns.zh: 哦，是啊。还有这一切。

turns.en: I'm just sort of– maybe sort of said a little bit here and I'm curious from think tank world. What do you think about so many social scientists, including a lot of economists, suddenly either leaving universities or leaving think tanks and joining one of two very big AI companies?
turns.zh: 我只是有点——也许这里已经说了一些——我很好奇，站在智库界（think tank world）的角度，你怎么看这么多社会科学家，包括很多经济学家，突然之间要么离开大学、要么离开智库，加入那两家非常大的 AI 公司中的一家？

turns.en: And when you think about.
turns.zh: 当你想到……

turns.en: The sort of future of social scientists, not so much like, well, we use models, which I'm sure there's going to be tons of that, but just the sort of Depending on which side you're on, either vortex or brain drain of people of stature moving into these companies.
turns.zh: 社会科学家的未来——倒不是说'我们用模型'这类事，那种我肯定会有大量需求——而是说，取决于你站在哪一边，这要么是一个漩涡（vortex），要么是一场人才流失（brain drain）：有分量的人纷纷进入这些公司。

turns.en: What do you think? How does that make you feel?
turns.zh: 你怎么看？这让你作何感想？

turns.en: I mean, as someone whose main job is to hire, develop, and retain talent, I think about this a lot. And it is, as I think you applied, Joe, I mean, I think it's not unprecedented. So during the internet boom, when Amazon was first coming up and Google was first coming up, they hired economists. They were hiring them more to be useful, like Amazon's pricing model, useful in terms of internal production. Design and auction system or something like that. Right. So like the very famous MIT microeconomist, Hal Varian, became Google's first chief economist and brought with him and hired a bunch of really smart people. But they also were there to talk about policy and help explain why the technology was good and what kinds of regulations they wanted and didn't want. And that's normal. I mean, that's okay. But there was also a little bit of this sense, which we're seeing now, an order of magnitude higher. Oh my God, I can make real money. Oh my God, that's where the cool people are. Oh my God, I can be part of changing the world. So it's very seductive. And we've seen this in other fields. When genetic engineering had a boomlet many decades ago, all these Nobel Prize winners and grad students would leave academic jobs and set up startups to Genentech, things like that. Right now, I think it's challenging. It's challenging because the case that can be made, and I know I have colleagues I know who have gone in-house at some of these companies. The case that can be made that this is the most transformative technology of a century. and it has the potential to do enormous good for the world, is legit. It may be overhyped, it may take longer to get there, we may have to care more about how many people we displace and what happens on the way, but the idea that that is a valid view and you want to be part of that, I think is real. And so beyond the money and the sense of I want to be doing the cool stuff, which matter, because think tanks, you pay well compared to average American salaries, which don't pay like those people. I understand it. You can also go one step further, which is unlike, say, Google or Amazon when they were coming up, where there were policy issues. Actually, a lot of us didn't realize what all the policy issues were. And the economists who were hired Some of them worked on policy, but most of them were, like we said, working on sort of internal tools. Now, a lot of what the hiring, say, for example, Anthropic is doing is by their own account about trying to envision what the right policies are to make the transition for AI work. And at least among the economists I know who've gone there, that's a sincere belief. But it does make it more awkward sometimes Because it's one thing to say, oh, I work for Amazon. I came up with the pricing auction model, and that's why you get that. And people say, you're ripping me off. And you say, no, I'm not. Ah, fine. But when it's like someone who's a world-class expert on the economics of innovation or of growth or whatever goes in and then starts saying, well, you know, they're going to create three times as many jobs as they destroy, and it's... The singularity is near, and so you can't regulate it right now because we're on the cusp of something. They may sincerely believe it, but it gets... People understandably discount their views once they're in-house and getting money. And also, and I was talking about this, a very noted academic who has been pursued by all these places who turned it down not to go. I mean... Hero. Well... And this is a person who's very techno-optimist. I mean, so it's not about that. But there's also just, you do inherently, these are still companies. I mean, you're becoming part of a hierarchy. You're losing your independent voice. What you choose to work on, you may choose not to work on that, which you might have worked on because now you work for this company. So again, is it outright corruption of the sort we're seeing in the Trump administration? No. But it is unsettling. And I think there's a role for this academic colleague of mine, the people at the Peterson Institute and like institutes to, I hope, be willing to settle for the low six-figure salaries, which are still pretty darn good, and influence policy without going on staff.
turns.zh: 作为一个主要工作就是招募、培养和留住人才的人，我对这个问题想得很多。而且，就像你说的，Joe，我觉得这并非史无前例。互联网繁荣期，Amazon 刚崛起、Google 刚崛起的时候，他们也雇经济学家。他们雇人更多是为了实用，比如 Amazon 的定价模型，用于内部生产、设计拍卖系统之类的。对吧。像那位非常有名的 MIT 微观经济学家 Hal Varian，成了 Google 的第一位首席经济学家，还带来并雇了一批非常聪明的人。但他们也在那里谈政策，帮忙解释为什么这项技术是好的、他们想要和不想要什么样的监管。这很正常。我是说，这没问题。但当时也有那么一点这种心态——而现在我们看到的心态，其强烈程度要高出一个数量级：'天啊，我能赚大钱了。天啊，酷的人都在这儿。天啊，我能参与改变世界了。'所以它非常有诱惑力。我们在别的领域也见过。几十年前基因工程有过一波小繁荣时，那些诺贝尔奖得主和研究生纷纷离开学术岗位去创办初创公司，像 Genentech 之类。现在，我觉得这是个挑战。之所以是挑战，是因为可以成立的一个论点——我认识一些已经去了这些公司内部（in-house）的同事——这个论点是：这是一个世纪以来最具变革性的技术，它有潜力为世界带来巨大的好处。这是站得住脚的。它可能被过度炒作，可能要更久才能实现，我们可能得更关注我们替代了多少人、以及一路上会发生什么，但'这是一种正当的看法，而你想参与其中'，我觉得是真实的。所以，除了钱、除了'我想做酷的事情'这种心态之外——这些都很重要，因为智库嘛，跟美国人的平均薪资比你付得不错，但付不到那些人（AI 公司）的水平——我理解。你还可以更进一步：跟当年 Google 或 Amazon 崛起时不同，那时其实有政策问题，只是我们很多人没意识到所有的政策问题是什么；而被雇的那些经济学家，有些做政策，但大多数、就像我们说的，是在做内部工具。而现在，比如说 Anthropic 招聘，按他们自己的说法，很大程度上是想弄清楚什么样的政策才对，才能让 AI 的转型顺利运转。至少在我认识的去了那儿的经济学家里，这是一种真诚的信念。但这有时确实让局面更尴尬。因为，说'哦，我在 Amazon 工作，我设计了定价拍卖模型，所以你才看到那个'是一回事——人们说'你在坑我'，你说'没有'，啊，好吧。但当一个世界级的创新经济学或增长经济学（或随便什么）专家进了公司，然后开始说'他们会创造的岗位是摧毁的岗位的三倍''奇点临近（the singularity is near）''所以现在没法监管，因为我们正处在某个突破的边缘'——他们也许真诚地相信，但这就……一旦他们进了公司内部、拿着钱，人们理所当然地会给他们的话打折扣。还有，我跟一位非常知名、被所有这些机构争相邀请、但拒绝去的学者聊过这个。我是说……英雄啊。嗯……而且这个人是非常的技术乐观派（techno-optimist）。所以这不是技术问题。但还有一点：本质上，这些仍然是公司。你在成为某个层级体系的一部分，你在失去你独立的声音。你选择研究什么——你可能就选择不研究某个东西了，而那本来你是可能会去研究的，因为现在你为这家公司工作。所以再说一次，这是我们 Trump 政府里看到的那种赤裸裸的腐败吗？不是。但它确实令人不安。我觉得，对于我这位学者同事、对于 Peterson Institute 以及类似机构的人来说，是有一个角色的：我希望他们愿意接受那种六位数偏低的薪水——那其实也相当不错了——在不进入公司任职的情况下去影响政策。

turns.en: Just on the AI side of things. So at the moment, if you look at the economic impact, it's very much sort of short-term effects on prices and inflation and capital investment. And everything else, you know, the impact on productivity, even jobs, is much further off into the future and very theoretical. Do you see any evidence of an impact on the labor market side or productivity here and now?
turns.zh: 就 AI 这一面来说。目前，如果你看它的经济影响，很大程度是对价格、通胀和资本投资（capital investment）的短期效应。而其它一切——你知道——对生产率、甚至对就业的影响，都还在很远的未来，非常理论化。你有没有看到任何证据，表明它此时此地对劳动力市场或生产率有影响？

turns.en: Much more indicative evidence of improvement in productivity, Tracy, than on effects on the labor market. So speaking of colleagues of mine, Martin Terzempa and Jed Kolko are both top economists who work at Peterson and work on these issues. Anton Koronek is affiliated with Peterson, is on leave this year. He went to work at Anthropic this year. But anyway, if you look at their work, and in particular, I would cite the work of Jed Kolko. And he was chief economist at the U.S. Department of Commerce under Biden. He was at Indeed, was it Indeed or ADP? Yeah, Indeed, I believe. Yeah, and yeah, so he's a real practical labor market economist. And he and there are a number of others, there's another think tank called economic innovation group. There are a bunch of them. And you're just not seeing it in the data. So the number of hires, even of coders, you know, if you had to pick the two jobs where you most thought they're toast, would be long haul truckers and coders, lower level coders. And we're just not seeing it. Job growth continues in those industries. I think there's been a lot of yes, theory, but really important theory work done, not by my team, but by people like Eric Bjornolfsson at Stanford or Luis Garicano at London School of Economics about why, those are just two examples, but they've done great work, about why we haven't seen the job displacement yet. And partly it's a matter of time, as you indicated. Time keeps coming up. It's how fast things happen. that there is arguably a period in which it is efficient to have the human and the AI working together, especially as the AI is in sort of learning mode, and especially as the businesses, just like with the internet, you have the technology and then you have to figure out how to reform your business to make use of it. So there's a period there, we don't know if it's one year, five years, it's probably less than 10 years, it's probably closer to five. But there's a period there where the businesses are changing, and the specialized applications are being created, and things like robotics are being integrated. And during that period, we probably don't lose many jobs. Again, long-haul truckers, I'm not trying to make fun of them. I mean, they may be the ones. And so Brynjolfsson has spoken about a J-curve, that it takes time for this to happen. And it's similar to the argument I made with you all about the effect of tariffs and migration last time I was on. Businesses, people have to make decisions and implement things. It takes time. Another argument which Luis Garcano and his co-authors have made is what they call messy jobs, which is the idea that actually, again, you can try to come up with the sort of extreme case long-haul trucker job, but almost every job, even arguably long-haul truckers, have... a lot more specific knowledge and are embedded in a lot of relationships that there's much more complicated and much more, I don't want to say uniqueness, but specialization than people appreciate. And so just sort of doing a lot of these things that get published by consulting firms or international institutions, like these are the most exposed sectors, these are the most exposed sectors, probably are misleading. And we know this from the past. Again, in the Industrial Revolution in 19th century England, the analog to the long-haul truck driver was the skilled artisan who did weaving. And so those people literally did get replaced by the automated weaving stuff. But if you had done this kind of study before the Industrial Revolution, outside of that very narrow, they're real people, but that very narrow job description, the displacement was very different than you would have expected. Anyway, so the job stuff, it's probably coming. If it is coming, it is showing up in the lack of hiring of younger people. Yeah, and Chair Warsh had a throwaway line in his speech yesterday, but it happens to be one I agree with, and again, we've talked about this previously, that a lot of the lack of hiring, I think, is overhang from the huge shifting around of people uh, and redefining jobs, um, after COVID and the re-employment. And so you can't automatically say the lack of hiring is AI. I mean, it may be contributing, but there's other stuff. Productivity is different. Um, so there, I think there's a legitimate active debate and it's not a debate ideologically or anything. It's cause it's generally, it's hard. You got a limited amount of data and you're trying to figure out what's going on. I think there's a legitimate debate about how much productivity growth we've got. That's due to AI. Is it the real big money stuff yet? How soon? I'm at probably just this side of pessimistic on that in the sense that I think going back to the jobs reshuffling after COVID, I don't think the AI productivity boost to growth kicked in until very recently, last year and a half. But that is much more an open debate. Nobody except some really, really crazy techno-optimists who talk about staying in your lane who are not economists. I think... You mean Joe? No, no, no, no, no. I would never say such a thing. He's a man for all seasons. Finally someone says that. I'm very diplomatic. I think the extreme calls... about huge amounts of productivity growth. As my grandmother used to say, we should be so lucky. But we ain't there yet.
turns.zh: 关于生产率改善的迹象性证据，Tracy，要比关于劳动力市场影响的证据多得多。说到我的同事，Martin Chorzempa 和 Jed Kolko 都是 Peterson 的顶级经济学家，研究这些问题。Anton Korinek 与 Peterson 有关联，今年休假，他今年去了 Anthropic 工作。总之，如果你看他们的研究，特别是我会引用 Jed Kolko 的工作。他在 Biden 任内是美国商务部（U.S. Department of Commerce）的首席经济学家。他在 Indeed 待过——是 Indeed 还是 ADP？对，我记得是 Indeed。是的，所以他是一位非常务实的劳动力市场经济学家。他，还有另外一批人——还有一个叫 Economic Innovation Group 的智库，有一堆人——你在数据里就是看不到那种影响。所以，招聘数量，哪怕是程序员（coders）——你知道，如果要挑两个你觉得最'完蛋'（toast）的职业，那会是长途卡车司机和初级程序员——我们就是没看到。这些行业的就业还在增长。我觉得已经有大量、是的、理论性但非常重要的研究——不是我团队做的，而是像 Stanford 的 Erik Brynjolfsson 或 London School of Economics 的 Luis Garicano 这样的人做的，那两个只是例子，他们做了很棒的工作——研究为什么我们还没看到岗位被替代。部分原因是时间问题，就像你指出的。时间这个因素总是冒出来，关键在于事情发生得多快。可以说，有一段时期，让人和 AI 协同工作是有效率的，尤其是当 AI 还处于'学习模式'时；尤其是企业——就像当年互联网一样——你有了技术，然后你得想办法改造你的业务来利用它。所以中间有那么一段时期，我们不知道是一年、五年，可能不到十年，可能更接近五年。但在那段时期里，企业在转型，专门的应用在被创造出来，机器人技术（robotics）之类的在被整合进来。在那段时间，我们大概不会失去很多岗位。同样，长途卡车司机——我不是想拿他们开玩笑——我是说，他们可能就是最先受影响的。所以 Brynjolfsson 讲过一个 J 曲线（J-curve），就是说这发生需要时间。这跟我上次上节目时跟你们讲的关于关税和移民影响的那个论点类似：企业、人都得做决定、去落实，这需要时间。Luis Garicano 和他的合著者提出的另一个论点，是他们所说的'杂乱的工作'（messy jobs）：这个想法是，其实——同样，你可以试着举出那种极端的例子，长途卡车司机这份工作——但几乎每一份工作，甚至可以说连长途卡车司机也一样，都……拥有多得多的专门知识，都嵌在大量关系里，比人们所认为的要复杂得多、也（我不想说'独特性'，而是）专门化得多。所以，很多由咨询公司或国际机构发布的、说'这些是最受冲击的行业、那些是最受冲击的行业'的东西，很可能是误导性的。我们从历史中就知道这一点。同样，在 19 世纪英国的工业革命中，长途卡车司机的类比对象，是那些做织布的技术工匠。那些人确实被自动织布的东西取代了。但如果你在工业革命之前做这类研究，除了那个非常狭窄的——他们是真实存在的人，但那个非常狭窄的职业描述之外——实际的替代情况会和你预期的非常不同。总之，就业方面的影响，它大概会来。如果它要来，它正体现在年轻人招聘的减少上。是的，Warsh 主席昨天演讲里有一句随口带过的话，但恰好是我认同的一句——我们之前也聊过这个——我认为很多招聘减少，其实是 COVID 之后人员大规模重新洗牌、岗位重新定义、以及重新就业所遗留的'余波'（overhang）。所以你不能想当然地说招聘减少就是 AI 造成的。我是说，它可能有一份贡献，但还有别的因素。生产率则是另一回事。呃，所以在生产率上，我觉得有一场正当的、活跃的辩论，而且这不是意识形态之类的辩论，而是因为这件事本身就难：你手上的数据有限，却要弄清楚到底发生了什么。我觉得关于我们目前有多少生产率增长是 AI 带来的，存在一场正当的辩论。它是那种真正'赚大钱'的东西了吗？还要多久？在这一点上，我大概偏向悲观这一侧一点点，我的意思是，回到 COVID 之后就业的重新洗牌，我觉得 AI 对增长的生产率提振直到最近、也就是过去一年半，才真正开始显现。但那更多是一场开放的辩论。除了某些非常非常疯狂的技术乐观派——那些不是经济学家、还大谈'待在你自己的赛道里'（staying in your lane）的人——没人会……你是说 Joe 吗？不不不不不。我绝不会那么说。他是个八面玲珑的人（a man for all seasons）。终于有人这么说了。我可是很外交辞令的。我觉得那些关于生产率大幅增长的极端判断……就像我奶奶常说的，'要真能那样我们该多走运'。但我们还没到那一步。

turns.en: I think, by the way, I find the messy jobs theory to be quite compelling. And by the way, the long haul truckers would absolutely say, look, there's a lot more to this job.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我觉得'杂乱的工作'（messy jobs）这个理论相当有说服力。而且顺便说一句，长途卡车司机绝对会说，听着，这份工作要做的远不止开车。

turns.en: Oh, I agree.
turns.zh: 哦，我同意。

turns.en: And include, you know, like all the things.
turns.zh: 而且包括，你知道，所有那些……

turns.en: That they have to do at the warehouse. No, I didn't mean to.
turns.zh: ……他们在仓库里要做的事。不，我不是有意（打断）的。

turns.en: No, no, I know. But I think it illustrates that point. Let me tell you what's actually involved.
turns.zh: 不不，我知道。但我觉得这恰好说明了那个观点。让我告诉你实际都涉及些什么。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Another one.
turns.zh: 还有一个。

turns.en: People point out, Adam Uzimek has pointed out that people still get hired to play the piano at parties.
turns.zh: 有人指出，Adam Ozimek 指出过，人们仍然会雇人在派对上弹钢琴。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。

turns.en: But as others would argue, well, the person responds to the crowd, they see what the mood is. These things that the player piano could not do, they could say like, oh, maybe this crowd looks like it needs an uptempo thing. So I do think these jobs are much more probably complex.
turns.zh: 但就像其他人会反驳的，嗯，那个人会根据现场观众做反应，他们能看出气氛如何。这些是自动钢琴（player piano）做不到的，他可以说，哦，也许这群人看起来需要来点快节奏的曲子。所以我确实觉得，这些工作很可能要复杂得多。

turns.en: I'm glad to hear you say that. And again, I was using the truckers just because that's the example everybody uses. But I agree with you. And Adam Ozemek, who's at EIG, is one of the other people. I think he's doing great work on this and comes down in this sort of, it may come yet, but it hasn't happened yet. But I think the really important point you said about the messy jobs is like with the piano. So I was in a meeting, supposed to be off the record, I won't go into details. but a very big, big, big, big, big shot from the AI community, not an economist. There are no economists big shots. From the AI community was talking, and a pretty famous academic economist asked this person, well, you kept telling everyone there's going to be a job apocalypse. Hasn't happened. Why do you think that is? Just open question. And among other things, this person said, the big, big, big, big shot said, Well, you know, it turns out people really like dealing with humans and don't always want to deal with machines. And even among the not exactly emotional IQ high economist community, we're all kind of like, duh. You know, I mean, that's what you mean about the live piano player. I mean, I didn't need AI to have Spotify. I mean, current generation AI to have Spotify, you know, like figure out if I like Paul Simon and Billy Joel. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我很高兴听你这么说。同样，我举卡车司机只是因为那是人人都在用的例子。但我同意你。而在 EIG 的 Adam Ozimek 是另一位，我觉得他在这方面做了很棒的工作，得出的结论大致是：它可能终究会来，但目前还没发生。不过我觉得你说的关于'杂乱的工作'那个真正重要的点，就像弹钢琴那件事。有一次我参加一个会议，本该是不对外记录（off the record）的，我不细说。但一位 AI 圈子里非常、非常、非常、非常、非常有分量的人物——不是经济学家，经济学家里没有大人物——来自 AI 圈的，在讲话。一位挺有名的学院派经济学家问这个人：'你一直跟大家说会有一场就业末日（job apocalypse）。可它没发生。你觉得为什么？'就是个开放性问题。除了别的，这个人——这位非常非常有分量的人物——说：'嗯，你知道，结果发现人们其实很喜欢跟人打交道，并不总想跟机器打交道。'哪怕在我们这个情商（emotional EQ）并不高的经济学家圈子里，我们都有点像'这还用说（duh）'。你知道，我是说，这就是你说的现场钢琴演奏者的意思。我是说，我要有 Spotify，并不需要 AI——我是说不需要当前这一代 AI——来帮我搞清楚我是不是喜欢 Paul Simon 和 Billy Joel。是啊。

turns.en: Since we're talking about some of these questions and measurement and limited data, I wanted to get your take on, I think you may have, I don't know if you saw it, there are these questions about, it came up with Nvidia specifically, and whether.
turns.zh: 既然我们在聊这些问题，还有测量和数据有限的话题，我想听听你的看法。我觉得你可能——我不知道你有没有看到——有一些疑问，具体是围绕 Nvidia 出现的，关于是否……

turns.en: Some of the chips that they design, but.
turns.zh: ……他们设计的一部分芯片，但……

turns.en: Which are manufactured elsewhere, largely Taiwan, et cetera, whether they're being adequately captured in data. And there was this report out that we should have added 0.3% to GDP. which is not that much in the sense that like, oh, the big techno-optimists were right.
turns.zh: ……那些在别处制造、主要是在 Taiwan 等地方的芯片，它们是否被充分地计入了数据。有一份报告说，我们本该给 GDP 加上 0.3%。这个数字不算大，不至于说'哦，那些大技术乐观派说对了'。

turns.en: No, but it's real money.
turns.zh: 不，但那是实打实的钱。

turns.en: I'm curious what you think. It is real money.
turns.zh: 我很好奇你怎么看。这确实是实打实的钱。

turns.en: On the other hand, when I look at it, I say, well, the market certainly noticed that NVIDIA has been doing very well. The Fed doesn't target GDP, so it doesn't really imply anything about, oh, we would have done something different monetary policy-wise.
turns.zh: 另一方面，当我看这件事时，我会说，嗯，市场当然已经注意到 NVIDIA 一直表现得非常好。Fed 并不以 GDP 为目标，所以它其实并不意味着'哦，我们在货币政策上本来会做些不同的事'。

turns.en: Tell us what your thoughts on this discussion are.
turns.zh: 跟我们说说你对这场讨论的想法吧。

turns.en: So, I mean, GDP, measuring how much income, we get for how much production and how much labor. That's what GDP is meant to do on a national basis. And it is much more science than art. But there are pieces of it where it's not very simple. And so there are multiple definitions. There's something called GDI, and then there's, of course, final demand, and there's these various things. And they're all meant to be a check on each other. And over time, they basically move together. So what you're saying, Joe, about this discussion of mismeasurement of say NVIDIA or the other top tech companies, again, doesn't really change the fundamental path. But going back to what you both raised, if we're trying to assess how much we've seen a big transformation in productivity, this matters. If this 0.3% say a year was overlooked and it is directly attributable to the AI sector, then that tells a different story about productivity. So it does matter. A colleague of mine I already mentioned, Martin Chorzempa at Peterson, is doing some work on this. Former Fed official at Peterson, Joe Gagnon, has also written about this. I mean, there are a lot of subtleties, which I don't even understand. But there are basically two issues. One is sometimes when companies that are based in the US, using US technology, produce stuff abroad, the allocation of how much stuff is actually produced in the U.S. versus not, and therefore how, whether it's GDP versus GNP, what's imports, what's exports, gets messed up. And so with these very complicated supply chains, there is an issue of trying to figure out what stuff gets allocated to the domestic pile versus the import pile.
turns.zh: 我是说，GDP，衡量的是我们用多少生产、多少劳动，换来多少收入。这就是 GDP 在国家层面本该做的事。它更多是科学而非艺术。但其中有些部分并不那么简单。所以有多种定义。有一个叫 GDI 的东西，然后当然还有最终需求（final demand），以及各种其它口径。它们本意是互相校验。随着时间推移，它们基本上一起变动。所以你说的，Joe，关于 NVIDIA 或其他顶级科技公司被测量错误（mismeasurement）的这场讨论，同样不会真正改变基本路径。但回到你们俩提出的点，如果我们要评估生产率到底出现了多大的转变，这一点就重要了。如果比如说每年这 0.3% 被漏掉了，而它可以直接归因于 AI 部门，那它就会讲出一个关于生产率的不同故事。所以它确实重要。我已经提到的一位同事，Peterson 的 Martin Chorzempa，正在做这方面的研究。Peterson 的 Fed 前官员 Joe Gagnon 也写过相关内容。我是说，这里有很多微妙的地方，连我自己都不完全理解。但基本上有两个问题。一个是，有时候当一家总部在美国、使用美国技术的公司在海外生产东西时，到底有多少东西实际是在美国生产的、有多少不是，这个分配——因而到底是算 GDP 还是 GNP、什么是进口、什么是出口——就被搞乱了。所以在这些非常复杂的供应链下，就存在一个问题：得弄清楚哪些东西被归到'国内'那一堆、哪些被归到'进口'那一堆。

turns.en: This is the old value-add argument.
turns.zh: 这就是那个老生常谈的'增加值'（value-add）论点。

turns.en: Yeah, sort of. Again, I'm worried I'm going to screw up on nuance. So look on our website for a paper by Joe or a paper by Joe Gagnon or Martin Shurzemba or Tweet. I'm afraid I don't want to. But just essentially, there is a discussion over how much is domestic versus national. But as you said, Joe, in the end, the market's you're either selling stuff or you're not. I mean, NVIDIA's bottom line actually doesn't change based on any of this. And the bottom line.
turns.zh: 对，差不多。同样，我担心自己会在细节上讲错。所以去我们网站上看 Joe——Joe Gagnon 或 Martin Chorzempa——的论文或推文吧。抱歉我不想讲错。但本质上，就是关于有多少算'国内'（domestic）、多少算'国民'（national）的讨论。但就像你说的，Joe，说到底，市场就是：你要么把东西卖出去了，要么没有。我是说，NVIDIA 的底线利润（bottom line）其实不会因为这些而改变。而且这个底线……

turns.en: We all know they're making a ton of money regardless of what the government does.
turns.zh: 我们都知道，不管政府怎么做，他们都在赚大钱。

turns.en: Also, the people who are working at NVIDIA designing the chips in the U.S. are still getting paid in debts.
turns.zh: 而且，那些在美国为 NVIDIA 设计芯片的人，仍然照样领薪水。

turns.en: Absolutely. And all the money that comes into NVIDIA, some of it goes to the shareholders, some of it goes to investments, some of it goes to the workers. So again, this is worth worrying about, but this is not a major distortion. The second thing, though, which is the more contentious part, is there are always, in technological revolutions, there are recurrent statements that GDP or whatever economists are using are just not capturing the true value. And usually the economist's response to that is some combination of, A, well, we're capturing the true market value. So if people are getting more out of it than what they're paying the markets, great. but the market value is what we're supposed to think about. That's one response. The second response is, oh, well, there are these various things like hedonic indexing where we try to adjust for quality. This shows up more on the inflation side than the growth side, but that helps you figure out what's real growth and what's not. So let's look at this specific sector and try and fix that. So there is still a controversy about that. I mean, but this goes back, Tracy, to what you were saying about the timing and the productivity or the J curve, right? So we already have GPT, GLAW, whatever. I don't want to cite any particular brand name. We have the AI. And You or I can go in and type, get me the cheapest possible ticket to Jackson Hole. I don't want to have to think about it, but don't seat me next to a baby. And that provides utils to me.
turns.zh: 完全正确。而且所有流入 NVIDIA 的钱，一部分给了股东，一部分用于投资，一部分给了员工。所以同样，这值得关注，但它不是一个重大的扭曲。不过第二点，也是更有争议的部分：在每一次技术革命中，总会反复出现这样的说法——GDP 或者经济学家所用的任何指标，根本没有捕捉到真正的价值。通常经济学家对此的回应是以下几种组合：一是，'我们捕捉的是真正的市场价值。所以如果人们从中得到的比他们付给市场的多，那很好，但市场价值才是我们该关注的。'这是一种回应。第二种回应是，'哦，有各种方法，比如享乐指数（hedonic indexing），我们用它来对质量做调整。'这更多体现在通胀一侧而非增长一侧，但它能帮你弄清楚什么是真实增长、什么不是。所以让我们看看这个具体的行业，试着把它修正一下。关于这一点仍然存在争议。我是说，但这又回到了你，Tracy，说的关于时点、生产率、或者 J 曲线的问题，对吧？所以我们已经有了 GPT、GLAW 之类的——我不想提任何具体的品牌名。我们有了 AI。然后你或我可以进去输入：'给我订一张去 Jackson Hole 尽可能便宜的机票，我不想费脑子，但别把我安排在婴儿旁边。'这就给我提供了效用（utils）。

turns.en: Tracy, when she does it, and she says, don't seat me next to Joe. Don't seat me next to Joe.
turns.zh: Tracy 做这个的时候，她会说，别把我安排在 Joe 旁边。别把我安排在 Joe 旁边。

turns.en: I thought it was don't seat me next to economists.
turns.zh: 我还以为是'别把我安排在经济学家旁边'呢。

turns.en: But we spend enough time together. Do we really need another four hours on a plane?
turns.zh: 可我们在一起的时间已经够多了。我们真需要在飞机上再来四个小时吗？

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不用。

turns.en: Keep going.
turns.zh: 你接着说。

turns.en: No, no, no, no. And so that's giving me utils. It's saving me some time. It gets me a better experience. I don't get annoyed with the AA or United or Delta website because somebody else is dealing with it for me. Does that show up in GDP? No. So this is why we usually think the big productivity gains and the disinflation stuff comes further down the pipeline. It's when we're on the track, I should say, not the pipeline. When the businesses start transforming. So like It was really cool that Intel and Texas Instruments and whoever else was building chips in the 90s were following Moore's Law and all that, and that showed up a bit in the GDP. But the gains really happened when McDonald's and Walmart and UPS and everybody transformed their businesses to take advantage of it.
turns.zh: 不，不，不，不。所以那是在给我提供效用。它帮我省了些时间，给了我更好的体验。我不会因为 AA、United 或 Delta 的网站而恼火，因为别人替我搞定了。这会体现在 GDP 里吗？不会。所以这就是为什么我们通常认为，大的生产率收益和去通胀（disinflation）效应，会出现在更靠后的环节。我应该说是在'轨道'（track）上，而不是'管道'（pipeline）上。是当企业开始转型的时候。就像，90 年代 Intel、Texas Instruments 还有其他造芯片的公司遵循摩尔定律（Moore's Law）等等，那真的很酷，也在 GDP 里体现了一点。但真正的收益，是当 McDonald's、Walmart、UPS 以及所有其他企业都转型去利用它的时候才出现的。

turns.en: Joe, do you remember when Goldman Economist, I think it might even have been Hatsies. Yeah, they put out a note saying that productivity was being mismeasured because the graphics in the new Grand Theft Auto game, I can't remember what edition it was at that time, were so much better than the previous graphics. We should have them back on now that the new one's coming out.
turns.zh: Joe，你还记不记得，有一次 Goldman 的经济学家——我觉得可能还是 Hatzius——发了一份报告，说生产率被测量错了，因为新版 Grand Theft Auto 游戏里的画面——我记不清当时是哪一代了——比之前的画面好太多。（现在新一代要出了，我们应该让他们再发一次。）

turns.en: Because the new GTA 6 is coming out. Yeah, we should do that.
turns.zh: 因为新的 GTA 6 就要出了。是啊，我们应该让他们再发一次。

turns.en: All right. I have just one more question. We could talk for hours, and unfortunately we don't have that much time, but Just in terms of the pure inflation outlook, the last time we had you on, it was right after you published a paper saying that you thought inflation was going to be 4% by the end of the year. I can't remember if you were looking at PCE or CPI.
turns.zh: 好的。我还有最后一个问题。我们能聊上几个小时，可惜我们没那么多时间。不过，就纯粹的通胀前景而言，上一次请你来，是在你刚发表一篇论文之后，你说你认为到年底通胀会到 4%。我记不清你看的是 PCE 还是 CPI 了。

turns.en: No, I was saying at that time, I was saying 4% on PCE and a little higher on CPI. Yeah. Okay.
turns.zh: 不，我当时说的是，PCE 是 4%，CPI 略高一点。是的。好的。

turns.en: Well, I mean, at least on CPI, we got to over 4% earlier in the year. And I think a lot of people were surprised by that direction of travel. What's your thinking now?
turns.zh: 嗯，我是说，至少在 CPI 上，今年早些时候我们确实到了 4% 以上。我觉得很多人对这个走向感到意外。你现在的想法是什么？

turns.en: I guess, thank you for citing that, Tracy. I guess what I was saying, and it was things I was saying and then a joint piece with Peter Orszag of Lazard, what we were saying was, going back to where we were with the criticisms of the PALFED that I think were legitimate, the U.S. labor market is much more resilient than they thought. Credit was much more available in the terms, the financial conditions were not as tight as they thought. Fiscal policy was a little looser than we thought. And the Fed, having not brought down inflation for 64 months or whatever it was then, 55 months, did have some momentum built up. And then additionally, one thing we talked about was, as I said, I think there was a J curve in the impact of tariffs and anti-migration policies, over time, it took time for it to kick in. But anyway, the big point was, whenever the next inflation shock comes, it's gonna go worse. I had no idea that the President of the United States would bomb Iran and ignore the fact that disrupting the Straits of Hormones might have some inflationary effects beyond whatever else you think of it. But I knew there was gonna be an inflation shock and we were primed to have more. So, the next couple months, inflation may trickle down a tenth or two because of the energy market, whatever. But as Chair Warsh said, as many FOMC members have said, this is not good. You've got persistence. You've got persistent inflation and essentially the core measures that are services and not imported goods. You've got, as the chair cited in his speech, you've got three, six, 12 months where The moving average looks like it's going up. It's in the high threes rather than four, but it's going up. So my view is the Fed is going to hike. If they don't hike in September, they're certainly going to hike in December. I expect if they hike in September, they're still going to hike in December. And so six months from now, Fed funds will be 75 pips or 100 pips higher than it is now. And inflation will start coming down for reals, as the kids say. But until then, we're going to be in this three and a half to four and a half range with some upside risk. All right.
turns.zh: 我想，谢谢你引用那段，Tracy。我想我当时说的——那是我自己说的一些观点，还有和 Lazard 的 Peter Orszag 合作的一篇文章——我们说的是，回到我们之前对那些对 Fed 的批评、我认为那些批评是正当的：美国劳动力市场比他们想的更有韧性；信贷的可得性要高得多，金融条件没有他们想的那么紧；财政政策比我们想的要更宽松一点；而 Fed，在 64 个月——或者说当时是 55 个月——没能把通胀压下来之后，确实积累了一些惯性（momentum）。此外，我们谈到的另一点是，就像我说的，我觉得关税和反移民政策的影响存在一个 J 曲线，随时间推移，它需要时间才会显现。但总之，关键点是：每当下一次通胀冲击来临，情况都会更糟。我完全没想到美国总统会去轰炸 Iran，还无视扰乱 Strait of Hormuz 可能带来的通胀影响——且不论你对这件事本身怎么看。但我知道会有一次通胀冲击，而我们已经'蓄势待发'、准备迎来更多。所以，接下来几个月，通胀可能因为能源市场之类的原因小幅回落零点一、零点二。但正如 Warsh 主席所说、正如许多 FOMC 委员所说，这不好。你有持续性（persistence）——你有持续的通胀，本质上是服务和非进口商品那部分的核心指标。而且，正如主席在演讲中引用的，你有三个月、六个月、十二个月的移动平均（moving average）看起来都在往上走。它处于接近 4% 的'高 3%'区间（high threes），而不是 4%，但它在往上。所以我的看法是，Fed 会加息。如果他们九月不加息，那十二月肯定会加。我预计，即便他们九月加了，十二月还是会加。所以六个月后，联邦基金利率（Fed funds）会比现在高 75 个基点或 100 个基点（pips）。而通胀会开始真正地回落，就像年轻人说的'for reals'。但在那之前，我们会一直处于这个 3.5% 到 4.5% 的区间，还带一些上行风险。好的。

turns.en: Adam Posen, always great catching up with you, especially this beautiful location.
turns.zh: Adam Posen，跟你叙旧总是很开心，尤其是在这么美的地方。

turns.en: Thank you so much for coming back on Outbox.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你再次来做客 Odd Lots。

turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: Love to hear it. Thank you.
turns.zh: 很高兴听你这么说。谢谢。

turns.en: Tracy, I love chatting with Adam. It's so good. It's always really good. I'm really glad we made it happen. You know what's interesting?
turns.zh: Tracy，我特别喜欢跟 Adam 聊天。太好了。每次都很棒。我真的很高兴我们促成了这次。你知道什么有意思吗？

turns.en: I'll be curious, like, to see how Powell's legacy ages. Like, I think there's going to be, you know, as Kevin Wurst said, 64, 65 months of above-target inflation. When you think back at the last several Fed shares, a lot of generally, like, the one who people, like, really think that was a bad tenure was Arthur Burns, right? Despite, and Bernanke is held up, like people think of him fondly, despite the fact that he presided over a financial crisis and several years.
turns.zh: 我会很好奇，想看看 Powell 留下的历史评价会经得起时间考验到什么程度。我是说，我觉得会是这样，你知道，就像 Kevin Warsh 说的，64、65 个月的通胀高于目标。回想过去几任 Fed 主席，大体上，那个大家真觉得任期很糟的，是 Arthur Burns，对吧？尽管……而 Bernanke 被树为正面典型，人们对他的评价很好，尽管他任内经历了一场金融危机和好几年的……

turns.en: Of high unemployment.
turns.zh: ……高失业率。

turns.en: It doesn't seem like from a reputational perspective, High unemployment under your watch gets sort of penalized the same degree as high inflation.
turns.zh: 从声誉的角度看，你任内的高失业率，似乎并不会受到和高通胀同等程度的'惩罚'。

turns.en: People really seem to hate inflation.
turns.zh: 人们似乎真的很痛恨通胀。

turns.en: You're right.
turns.zh: 你说得对。

turns.en: Like, it's kind of skewed.
turns.zh: 就是，这有点失衡（skewed）。

turns.en: Yeah, it clearly is.
turns.zh: 是啊，显然是。

turns.en: So, you know, between, like, the questions like, well, did the Fed gather this sense of momentum where people were not dissenting for maybe reasons that were sort of inevitable or structural, etc.? and you go over five years of above-target inflation. I just think it'll be really interesting to see how people are talking about Powell in the years ahead.
turns.zh: 所以，你知道，一方面是诸如'Fed 是否形成了这种大家都不投反对票的惯性，其原因也许是某种必然的或结构性的因素'这类问题；另一方面是你有超过五年的通胀高于目标。我只是觉得，未来几年人们会如何谈论 Powell，会非常有意思。

turns.en: It was also interesting to hear that there seems to be a sort of unspoken norm that you can only have a handful.
turns.zh: 听到这个也很有意思：似乎存在一种不成文的规范，就是每次会议只能有寥寥几个人……

turns.en: Of dissents per meeting. Yeah, I think it's... Oh, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: ……投反对票。是啊，我觉得这……哦，是啊，是啊。

turns.en: The other thing I was thinking about, just on the messy jobs note, I was... But I was thinking, so my husband and I, we were doing a project where we were roofing an outdoor shed and we asked ChatGPT how to do it. And we watched a couple of YouTube videos and it told us to use this one product, like to stick on the shingles and things. And then after we had started doing it, we realized that that product only worked in environments that were above 60 degrees Fahrenheit and we were in New England. And the bots and the YouTube videos were incapable of spotting that we were in fact in Connecticut versus Florida. So, you know, there's some nuance left for humans.
turns.zh: 我还在想另一件事，就着'杂乱的工作'这个话题。你知道，外面有种想法，觉得，哦，比如说，承包商（contractors）可以被取代，因为现在你只要问一下 ChatGPT，该怎么——我不知道——修你的马桶之类的。但我在想，我和我丈夫，我们当时在做个项目，给一个户外的棚屋铺屋顶，我们就问了 ChatGPT 怎么做。我们看了几个 YouTube 视频，它告诉我们要用某一种产品，用来粘那些屋顶板（shingles）之类的。然后等我们开始动手之后，才发现那种产品只在高于华氏 60 度（60 degrees Fahrenheit）的环境里才管用，而我们在 New England。那些机器人和 YouTube 视频根本没法识别出，我们其实是在 Connecticut，而不是 Florida。所以，你知道，还是给人类留下了一些需要拿捏的细微之处。

turns.en: Yeah, I think that's right.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得没错。

turns.en: I feel strongly like for all the extraordinary things that the models can do that, There are just so many of these minor things that we don't even articulate about what human judgment looks like that they're not there yet. They may yet get there. They may get there by the end of the year. But they're not quite there yet. But just like on the conversation, I do think it's interesting. You know, the term that I've been thinking about with the war speech.
turns.zh: 我强烈感觉，尽管这些模型能做那么多非凡的事情，但关于'人类判断力到底长什么样'，有太多这种细枝末节、我们甚至都说不清的东西，所以它们还没到那一步。它们也许终究会到，也许年底就能到。但它们现在还没完全到。不过就这场对话来说，我确实觉得有意思。你知道，关于 Warsh 那场演讲，我一直在想的那个词……

turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯嗯。

turns.en: I found it to be hawk-ish, which is like with a dash between the hawk and the ish, as in it was clearly more like, yes, clear that there's a plan to fight and that there is going to be work to do to get inflation because he said the two things that were key, which is inflation is going in the wrong direction and policy has been insufficiently restricted, which therefore the third thing that the silent part is, therefore high grades, which he didn't say.
turns.zh: 我觉得它是'鹰派倾向'（hawk-ish）——就是在 hawk 和 ish 之间加个连字符那种——意思是，它显然更像是：是的，很清楚有一个抗击通胀的计划，也很清楚要把通胀压下来还得下功夫，因为他说了两件关键的事，即通胀正朝着错误的方向走、而政策一直不够紧缩；因此第三件、也就是那个没说出口的部分是，因此要加息——而这句话他没说。

turns.en: So like, That is hawkish.
turns.zh: 所以，那确实算是鹰派。

turns.en: On the other hand, it was not hawkish in the sense that we are now about to embark on an aggressive... It was not Palo 2022, where it's just, we're going to get inflation down and I'll see you next year.
turns.zh: 另一方面，它又不是那种'我们现在就要大举……'的鹰派。它不是 2022 年的 Powell，那种'我们就是要把通胀压下去，明年见'。

turns.en: Well, it also begs the question of, okay, you could have said the exact same things at the July meeting, and yet he opted not to hike because he said he wanted to see more information. But more information is always coming out. And also in this environment, it feels like more shocks are also constantly happening. And so I, you know, you have to wonder what the threshold actually is. Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯，它还引出了一个问题：好吧，你完全可以在七月那次会议上说一模一样的话，可他却选择不加息，因为他说他想看到更多信息。但更多信息是永远都在冒出来的。而且在这种环境下，感觉冲击也在不断发生。所以，你知道，你不得不想知道，那个门槛到底是什么。是啊。
